content_metadata.description: A documentary showcasing the transformation of the healthcare system in Sierra Leone, focusing on the construction of the Maternal Center of Excellence and the existing Special Care Baby Unit at Koidu Government Hospital. It highlights the positive impact of healthcare initiatives and the empowerment of women through employment and skills development.

qAndA.answer: The Maternal Center of Excellence is a new healthcare facility being constructed to improve maternal and child health in Kono, Sierra Leone.
qAndA.question: What is the Maternal Center of Excellence?

qAndA.answer: The construction involves collaboration between Partners In Health, local engineers, and healthcare professionals, with a significant percentage of women employed at the site.
qAndA.question: Who is involved in the construction of the Maternal Center of Excellence?

qAndA.answer: The Special Care Baby Unit at Koidu Government Hospital has dramatically reduced child mortality by providing essential care to premature and fragile babies.
qAndA.question: What is the impact of the Special Care Baby Unit?

scenes.contextualRelevance: The visuals of the construction site and John Green's emotional reaction highlight the significance of the Maternal Center of Excellence project and create a sense of hope.

narrativeProgression.description: Hank Green introduces the video and greets viewers from Sierra Leone.
The video transitions to a shot of the construction site of the Maternal Center of Excellence.
The video shows two women, Marie and Success, who are construction workers at the MCOE.
John Green expresses his emotional reaction to the project.

scenes.title: Introduction to the Maternal Center of Excellence

scenes.contextualRelevance: The scene emphasizes the importance of collaboration between PIH, the Sierra Leone Ministry of Health, and the local community in achieving positive healthcare outcomes.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Visual shift from a well-maintained hospital ward to a dilapidated room with dirt floors and exposed wiring. This visual contrast highlights the challenges faced before the partnership with PIH.

Addition of text overlay explaining the lack of resources and the dire state of the hospital before PIH's involvement. This reinforces the grateful mood by emphasizing the extent of the transformation.

narrativeProgression.description: Hank Green begins by explaining the initial state of the maternity ward at Koidu Government Hospital eight years ago.
The video shows the present-day maternity ward, now well-maintained and bustling with activity.
Dr. Bailor Barrie explains the improvements made to the hospital, including a functioning operating room, blood bank, and medical resident training program.
The video transitions to images of the hospital before PIH's involvement, showing dilapidated rooms and exposed wiring.

scenes.thematicElements: Healthcare transformation, Collaboration, Hope and resilience
scenes.title: Gratitude for Healthcare Transformation

videoEditingDetails.description: Text overlay: 'There was no consistent electricity, lots of exposed wiring, no consistent running water to sanitize hands or tools, no functioning bathrooms, no blood bank, very little medication, and no functioning operating room to perform emergency C-sections. As a result, there were almost no patients.'

Text overlay: 'The Ministry of Health's national budget amounted to around $7 per person per year, and so there were simply no resources to rebuild the hospital without support from Partners In Health.'

scenes.contextualRelevance: The scene sheds light on the disparities in healthcare access and resources, highlighting the ongoing need for improvements in the system.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Auditive shift from Dr. Bailor Barrie's positive account of the hospital's progress to Hank Green's sobering observation about the inadequate healthcare system.
Visual shift from the improved hospital ward to the exterior of the hospital, with a text overlay highlighting the shortage of ambulances. This visual emphasizes the need for continued support.

narrativeProgression.description: Hank Green shifts the focus to the current inadequacy of the healthcare system in Kono, despite the positive changes.
He points out the scarcity of maternal beds, serving a population of over 500,000 people.
Hank Green emphasizes the ongoing challenges, including the lack of ambulance services and essential drugs.
He concludes by stating that the situation is unacceptable and needs to be addressed.

scenes.thematicElements: Healthcare disparities, Social responsibility, Urgency and action
scenes.title: Acknowledging Ongoing Challenges

videoEditingDetails.description: Text overlay: '(and not nearly enough ambulances!)'

characterInteraction.description: They work closely together, highlighting the collaborative effort between healthcare professionals and engineers in building the MCOE.

scenes.contextualRelevance: The scene celebrates the progress made in constructing the MCOE, symbolizing hope and a brighter future for healthcare in Kono.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Visual shift from the existing hospital facilities to the construction site of the MCOE. This change introduces a sense of hope and optimism for the future.
Introduction of Isata Dumbuya, Head of Maternal Health, who speaks enthusiastically about the MCOE and its potential impact. Her passion and energy contribute to the excited mood.

narrativeProgression.description: Hank Green introduces the MCOE as a solution to the inadequate healthcare system in Kono.
The video shows a billboard with an artist's rendering of the completed MCOE, further building anticipation.
Hank Green describes the active construction taking place, emphasizing the progress being made.
Isata Dumbuya expresses her excitement about the MCOE and the positive impact it will have on maternal and child health.
Hank Green mentions the collaboration between PIH and local engineers to ensure the quality of the construction.

scenes.thematicElements: Progress and development, Community ownership, Investment in the future
scenes.title: Excitement for the Maternal Center of Excellence

characterInteraction.description: The interaction is respectful and appreciative. The women express their gratitude for the opportunities provided by the MCOE project and share their personal stories of growth and empowerment.

scenes.contextualRelevance: The scene promotes gender equality by showcasing women's active participation and success in a traditionally male-dominated field.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Auditive shift from discussing the construction progress to focusing on the training and empowerment of women working on the site. Hank Green's voice takes on a tone of admiration and respect.
Visual shift from the bustling construction site to a classroom setting, where women are learning new skills. This transition emphasizes the importance of education and training in the project.

narrativeProgression.description: Hank Green highlights the significant percentage of women working on the MCOE construction site.
He introduces Hawa, Marie, and Success, three women who have gained valuable skills and experience through the project.
Hawa shares her pride in her work and her excitement for the future opportunities it will provide.
Marie describes her journey from selling corn on the street to becoming a skilled welder.
Success explains how her experience as a mason led her to a new role as a steel binder.

scenes.thematicElements: Gender equality, Skills development, Personal transformation
scenes.title: Empowerment Through Construction Skills

videoEditingDetails.description: Text overlay: 'We go to YouTube University on TV!'
Text overlay: 'So I know the skills I’m learning are not only for today; it's for tomorrow.'
Text overlay: 'I am proud as a woman now.'
Text overlay: 'Anywhere I go, people will be proud of me, because they've never seen construction women before.'
Text overlay: 'They teach us to cut [steel], to weld … and now I am a welder.'
Text overlay: 'We know that one day we will give birth in this hospital. Our children will be coming here. So that’s why we try all effort to build this hospital.'

characterInteraction.description: They continue to collaborate, demonstrating the ongoing partnership between healthcare professionals and engineers. The young boys observing the construction symbolize future beneficiaries of the MCOE project.

scenes.contextualRelevance: The scene highlights the holistic approach of the MCOE project, addressing not only the physical building but also the supporting infrastructure, staff housing, and human resource development.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Visual shift from the women discussing their work to a wide shot of the construction site for dormitories and staff housing. This transition emphasizes the broader scope of the MCOE project.
Introduction of young boys observing the construction. This visual evokes a sense of hope and the positive impact the project will have on future generations.

narrativeProgression.description: Hank Green explains how Isata Dumbuya and her team are working closely with engineers to ensure the proper design of the MCOE.
The video shows the construction site for the dormitories and staff housing, highlighting the additional infrastructure being built.
Hank Green mentions the importance of housing for staff and students working at the MCOE.
He shifts the focus to the training of nurses and doctors, emphasizing the long-term investment in human resources.

scenes.title: Holistic Approach to Healthcare Infrastructure

characterInteraction.description: Isata Dumbuya guides Hank Green through the Special Care Baby Unit, explaining its operations and the dedication of the staff. Her expertise and passion for her work are evident in her interactions with Hank Green.

scenes.contextualRelevance: The scene showcases the life-saving interventions being provided through the Special Care Baby Unit, emphasizing the tangible impact of healthcare initiatives.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Visual shift from the construction site to the existing Special Care Baby Unit, highlighting the immediate impact being made on child health.
Auditive shift from discussing the need for ongoing support to focusing on the successes of the existing Special Care Baby Unit. Isata Dumbuya's voice conveys a sense of pride and accomplishment.

narrativeProgression.description: Hank Green introduces the Special Care Baby Unit as an example of the positive impact already being made.
Isata Dumbuya explains the unit's crucial role in providing care for premature and fragile babies.
The video shows the Special Care Baby Unit sign, emphasizing its significance within the hospital.
Hank Green acknowledges the unit's success in dramatically reducing child mortality.
He highlights the importance of skilled staff, training, and ongoing supplies in maintaining the unit's functionality.

scenes.thematicElements: Life-saving interventions, Capacity building, Hope and survival
scenes.title: Impact of the Special Care Baby Unit

videoEditingDetails.description: Text overlay: 'Electricity! Water! The list goes on and on and on because the WHOLE SYSTEM is involved.'

climax.description: The unveiling of the Maternal Center of Excellence, symbolizing a new era of healthcare for Sierra Leone.

storylines.description: The documentary traces the journey of healthcare improvements in Sierra Leone, focusing on the construction and impact of the Maternal Center of Excellence and the Special Care Baby Unit. It highlights the collaboration between Partners In Health, the Sierra Leone Ministry of Health, and the local community.

content_metadata.title: Journey to Healthcare Excellence in Sierra Leone

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Good morning Hank, it's Tuesday greetings from Sierra Leone and the maternal center of excellence.
So Hank, this is the 48,000 square foot maternal and infant care center currently being built in
Sierra Leone. These are a few of the women building it and this is my crying and sweaty face as it
sinks in how many lives are being helped by our little online community. But let me back up.
Eight years ago when partners in health began working with Sierra Leone's Ministry of Health to
strengthen the health care system in the Cono district, the maternity ward at Coydoo Government
Hospital did not look like this overflowing with new moms receiving excellent care with a functioning
operating room and blood bank and medical residents training to be the next generation of Sierra
Leone physicians. No eight years ago it looked like this. Dirt floors devoid of patients due to a
long history of impoverishment of horrific civil war and the collapse of the already fragile health
care system during the Ebola epidemic. What's been accomplished since is remarkable. Cono was the
epicenter of the world's maternal mortality crisis with one in 17 women dying in childbirth or
pregnancy, but that's changed. Both maternal and child mortality have declined dramatically.
Still the health care system in Cono remains inadequate. There are only 41 maternal beds to serve a
population of over 500,000 people, so the maternity ward is perpetually over full. And mothers
in children in Cono are still dying every day for want of emergency C-sections, ambulance services,
and drugs to combat postpartum hemorrhage. It's simply not acceptable. And also we don't have to
accept it. That's where the maternal center of excellence comes in, with help from the nearly
40 million dollars raised by Nerdfighteria and P.I.H. over the last three and a half years.
This will be the world-class health care center moms and kids deserve in Cono. Hank, it's impossible
to communicate the scale of this place with a camera, but footers are being poured,
dresses are being welded, plumbing, and wiring is going in, and the first wards will hopefully
open next year. I saw the Dombaya, the nurse midwife who leads maternal health at the hospital,
is working closely with build health international engineer John Chu and his team to make sure that
everything is right where it should be. John, by the way, has a phenomenal sharpy hat. At the
maternal center of excellence, there will not only be excellent maternal care, there will also be
two neonatal intensive care units, one for babies born in the hospital, another for babies born
outside, and brought to the hospital, as well as enough operating theaters and supplies to
perform up to 10 emergency C-sections every day. And the MCLE will also be a teaching hospital,
so a new generation of midwives, nurses, and doctors will train there. We also got to visit the
site where the dormitories and staff housing will be, and met some kids engaging in the time-honored
cross-cultural tradition of young boys watching big machines. But it's not only health care workers
who are learning and being trained via the MCLE, as John Chu explained to us, almost all the people
working on the construction site have been trained in new skills, partly via classes, and partly via
get this educational YouTube videos. We've got a YouTube University on TV.
65% of the construction workers on this site are women, and I got to chat with three of them,
including Hawa, who was selling corn on the street in Koydo before getting this job, and who now
has become an expert in reading blueprints and trains new workers on how to use tools.
I know the skill I'm learning is not only for teaching. She told me about how profoundly her life
has changed, but also about how she feels differently about herself. I'm glad I see women now.
Anywhere I go, I don't know if that'll make a difference. I never see the construction women before.
Marie has also been able to learn a highly skilled trade. She shows about two codes,
two where they're now, and where they're now. And success after working as a Mason on the site is
now a steel binder. She has a theory on why so many women are working at the MCOE.
But to be clear, I saw that her team aren't waiting on buildings to improve maternal and
child health. More nurses and doctors are already training at the existing facilities. More
community health workers are being hired to identify high-risk pregnancies via a house call,
and most astonishingly, a special care baby unit at the hospital has already dramatically
reduced child mortality. The idea is that they should always have access to their babies and be able to
to feed on demand as needed. Before we visited the unit, I sought to explain to us that as recently
as two years ago, the vast majority of these babies would have died. The unit is full, so full that
at times the team has to make unspeakably difficult decisions about who they can admit,
but the babies here receive excellent care, world-class care, the kind of care that every baby
deserves. There are many such special care baby units at hospitals around Sierra Leone,
but very few of them are functioning because it's not just about the building and supplying incubators.
It's also about the staff, the training, the ongoing supplies needed to run such a unit,
maintenance, and so much more. Because I saw that and her team have not just the building and
the incubators, but also the support they need to succeed, this unit is thriving. And so to the
thousands of you who donate monthly at pah.org slash hank and john and the thousands more who've
made one-time gifts to the people who've brought attention by sharing this project with friends and
family, this is the change you're making. Two years ago, the parents of almost all of these kids
would have gone home heartbroken, but the kind of dignified high-quality health care that everyone
deserves is coming to Cono and with it generational change. To properly support the MCOE and the
larger strengthening of Cono's health care system over the next few years, we still need to raise
the poultry sum of just over 10 million dollars. So we have a long way to go. If you can join the
monthly donors or make a one-time gift, check out pah.org slash hank and john. And if you're
considering making a large gift, we've had donations from $2,000 to $500,000, please give via the
special link below or email me with questions. And if you can't afford to donate, that's okay.
Thank you for your attention. It matters. If I've learned anything from the first three and a half
years of this project, it is this. Collectively, we are much more likely to solve the problems
that we pay attention to. When we were in the special care baby unit, partners and health
co-founder Ophelia Dahl asked a nurse if one especially frail baby on a CPAP machine was likely to live.
All these babies are going to live. The nurse responded. This is the Good News Room. I'm so proud
that KoiDoo government hospital now has a Good News Room. And with the work of Marie,
Hawa, Success, and so many others on the Maternal Center of Excellence, there is much more Good
News to come. Hank, look at what humans can do when we come together. I'll see you on Friday.

Make a monthly or one-time gift to support the MCOE and its mission to radically reduce maternal and child mortality: http://pih.org/hankandjohn
More ways to help:
1. If you can donate $2,000 or more, please join the matching fund via this link: https://www.pih.org/maternal-center-excellence?form=match-for-sierra-leone Or if you have questions about a major gift, you can email me at sparksflyup -at- gmail

2. Join the Awesome Coffee Club! http://awesomecoffeeclub.com or get Sun Basin soap: https://good.store/pages/sun-basin-soap

3. SPREAD THE WORD. Your attention matters. Keep up to date on what's happening in Sierra Leone via https://www.pihsierraleone.com/

In which John visits Sierra Leone's Kono District for the first time since Covid and is astonished by the progress, the hope, and how far we still have to go. THANK YOU THANK YOU THANK YOU to everyone who is working on the MCOE, who is strengthening the healthcare system in Sierra Leone, and also everyone who has donated, or joined the sock club, or bought soap, or spread the word about the ongoing global maternal mortality crisis. Really, thanks to all of you. Look what humans can do together.
